content:
Hi everyone,

I am putting together a benchmark project, Autoformalization for the Working Mathematician, and am looking for domain experts across all areas of mathematics, theoretical computer science, and theoretical physics to collaborate as consultants. Please sign up here if you are interested: signup

The Motivation

If we want to steer the development of AI tools in a direction that is genuinely beneficial for the practice of mathematics, we need benchmarks for tasks that can augment the research effort of ordinary mathematicians. Our goal is to construct formal proof outlines that follow known natural language proofs, and solving the benchmark problem means formalizing as many nodes of the outline as possible. Crucially, these formal outlines will be truncated—meaning solvers can assume certain background results without proof, mirroring standard mathematical literature.

What We Need

We are looking for experts to help construct sample problems. Specifically, we want theorems that are very challenging and are unlikely to be formalized by the Lean community in the near future.

Benchmark problems will be developed in collaboration between Lean experts and math domain experts. Please pass the word along to mathematicians who are not active in formalization but still might want to contribute.

Compensation

We recognize that this requires deep, specialized expertise. Consultants will be compensated at a rate of $200/hr for their time and effort. We thank DARPA’s expMath program for funding this effort.

Resources

Sample Problems: You can get a sense of the format we are aiming for in our pilot repository here: Autoformalization Pilot (Note: the current examples are just to demonstrate the format and are not as esoteric as the theorems we ultimately want to collect).

Project Philosophy: For a more thorough description of the motivation and philosophy behind the project, please take a look at these slides: Hoboken slides

If you care about shaping the next generation of mathematical tools and are interested in contributing, please fill out the form. We will be in touch soon.

Best,

Daniel Halpern-Leistner

https://danielhl.github.io/
This topic was moved here from #Project announcements > AWM Benchmark by Jireh Loreaux.

Specifically, we want theorems that are very challenging and are unlikely to be formalized by the Lean community in the near future.

What does "the Lean community" mean? Specifically, do you mean "theorems which are unlikely to end up in mathlib in the near future" (an extremely narrow interpretation of the phrase) or "theorems which are unlikely to be formalized by anyone in the world who may have access to frontier models or work for a big lab and who happens to post on the Lean Zulip" (an extremely wide interpretation)?

Edit: I think I've answered my own question by reading the README at https://github.com/DanielHL/autoformalization_pilot :

  • The problem should be unlikely to appear online in a human formalization project any time soon.

I'm not sure it's reasonable to define "the Lean community" as "people who will not use machines to do formalization" so perhaps the description above needs editing.
